title: Physical and logical topology
basic: Physical topology describes actual cables, radios and devices. Logical topology describes how traffic is organized and forwarded.
intermediate: Draw separate maps for physical links, VLAN membership and routed subnets. One physical switch can carry several logically separate networks.
advanced: An overlay can create logical connections across an underlay. Reachability depends on forwarding state and policy, not just a line in a diagram.
example: A Wi-Fi access point and wired switch can share one VLAN while using different physical media.
question: Does a cable between two devices guarantee application access?
answer: No. Link state, addressing, forwarding, firewall policy and application authorization all matter.

title: Point-to-point topology
basic: A single link connects two endpoints. It is easy to understand and troubleshoot.
intermediate: A routed connection between two routers is a common example. Distinguish a physical cable from a logical tunnel crossing several links.
advanced: One link has no alternate path on its own. Two parallel links may still share a cable duct, power supply or provider.
example: Remove the only link in the drawing: both endpoints lose that direct path.
question: Are two tunnels always independent?
answer: No. They can share the same underlying path and failure domain.

title: Bus topology
basic: Devices attach to one shared backbone. Classic coaxial Ethernet is a historical example.
intermediate: Attached stations share the medium. Cable termination and shared-medium access behavior matter in the relevant technology.
advanced: A backbone fault can affect many stations; outcome depends on the physical implementation. Modern switched Ethernet should not be described as a shared coaxial bus.
example: Draw four stations attached to one backbone and mark the backbone as a shared dependency.
question: Does every Ethernet network use bus topology?
answer: No. Switched Ethernet commonly uses point-to-point links in a physical star or tree.

title: Star topology
basic: Each endpoint connects to a central device, often an Ethernet switch or wireless access point.
intermediate: Failure of one endpoint cable typically isolates that endpoint. Failure of the central device can disconnect all attached endpoints.
advanced: A central hub and a switch can have the same physical star shape but different forwarding behavior. A switch does not inherently provide redundant power or paths.
example: For four computers attached to one switch, mark one cable failure and then a switch failure. Compare affected computers.
question: Does a star remove all single points of failure?
answer: No. The central device and its shared power or uplink may remain single points of failure.

title: Ring topology
basic: Each node has two neighbors in a closed loop. The physical ring does not define its forwarding protocol.
intermediate: Some ring technologies use token passing or protection mechanisms; ordinary Ethernet links arranged in a ring do not automatically provide either.
advanced: Redundant Layer 2 paths need loop prevention or a suitable protection design. An uncontrolled forwarding loop can circulate frames and disrupt the network.
example: Break one drawn edge: an undirected ring remains connected as a path, but real recovery depends on the protocol and configuration.
question: Will every ring survive any fault without interruption?
answer: No. Link direction, protection protocol, fault count and convergence behavior determine actual service continuity.

title: Full and partial mesh
basic: In a full mesh, every node connects directly to every other node. A partial mesh connects only selected pairs.
intermediate: A full mesh of n nodes needs n(n-1)/2 undirected point-to-point links. Five nodes need ten links; each node has four neighbors.
advanced: Extra paths increase redundancy and operational complexity. Routing or bridging rules must choose usable paths; connectivity alone is not a security policy.
example: Compare a four-node full mesh with six links against a partial mesh with five. Identify failures that disconnect each graph.
question: Does the formula count ports or cables?
answer: It counts pairwise links under the stated model. With one port per end, those links consume n(n-1) ports in total.

title: Tree and hierarchical topology
basic: A tree branches from a root through intermediate nodes to leaves. A simple tree has no cycles.
intermediate: Access switches can connect endpoints to distribution devices. An upstream failure affects the subtree that depends on it.
advanced: Real campus designs often add redundant uplinks and are no longer strict graph-theory trees. Document the actual active paths and failure domains.
example: Mark a failed distribution device and count only the leaves dependent on it.
question: Is every three-tier network a strict tree?
answer: No. Three-tier describes roles; redundant cross-links can make the physical graph cyclic.

title: Hybrid topology
basic: A hybrid combines patterns, such as stars joined through a partial mesh.
intermediate: Describe each region separately: endpoint access, building uplinks and inter-site connections. A single label can hide important dependencies.
advanced: Review shared power, upstream providers, control planes and security boundaries across regions. A visually redundant layout may share a hidden dependency.
example: Two office stars connect to a pair of routed backbone devices. Mark the endpoint, building and backbone failure domains.
question: How do you assess a hybrid network?
answer: Break it into regions, trace required traffic paths and examine failures and policy at every boundary.

title: Spine-leaf topology
basic: A common data-center design connects each leaf switch to every spine switch. Endpoints attach to leaves.
intermediate: In a typical routed fabric, traffic between leaves crosses a spine. Equal-cost multipath can distribute flows across available paths.
advanced: Capacity depends on link speeds, counts and traffic patterns. Aggregate offered traffic exceeding uplink capacity creates oversubscription; equal path counts do not imply equal bandwidth.
example: A leaf with eight equal-speed host links and two equal-speed uplinks has a nominal 4:1 host-to-uplink capacity ratio before overhead and traffic effects.
question: Is a spine-leaf fabric a full mesh of all switches?
answer: No. The usual leaf-to-spine pattern is bipartite: leaves connect to spines, not every switch to every other switch.

title: Wireless infrastructure and mesh
basic: Infrastructure Wi-Fi clients associate with access points. Wireless mesh can use radio links between infrastructure nodes.
intermediate: Distinguish client access from backhaul. Obstacles, interference and shared airtime influence performance even when all nodes are visible on a diagram.
advanced: Multi-hop paths can consume airtime repeatedly; a dedicated backhaul changes the tradeoff. Roaming, channel planning and authentication are separate design concerns.
example: Draw a client-to-access-point link and a separate backhaul link; label which radio or cable carries each.
question: Does mesh guarantee higher speed?
answer: No. Link quality, airtime, hop count, backhaul design and offered load determine performance.

title: Redundancy, loops and convergence
basic: Redundancy supplies alternatives. Resilience is the ability to continue or recover service under faults.
intermediate: Layer 2 loop-prevention mechanisms and Layer 3 routing solve different forwarding problems. Recovery requires detection and a valid alternate path.
advanced: Measure packet loss and recovery time as well as eventual connectivity. Two paths sharing one power source are not independent against a power failure.
example: On paper, remove one link and then one central node. Find a remaining path and list the assumptions needed to use it.
question: Can an extra cable reduce reliability?
answer: Yes. Without an appropriate forwarding design it can create loops or unintended paths.

title: Choosing and documenting a topology
basic: Start with required communication, endpoint count, distance, budget and acceptable downtime.
intermediate: Compare cabling cost, central dependencies, expansion, troubleshooting and bandwidth. Place routing and firewall boundaries deliberately.
advanced: Record both expected and observed behavior, including shared failure domains and convergence limits. Update diagrams after changes and validate using approved evidence.
example: Create a fictional office design with staff, guest and IoT segments; explain allowed flows and what happens if the access switch fails.
question: Does a VLAN diagram prove isolation?
answer: No. You must also verify routing, filtering, service exposure and the actual configuration.
